title: Cover the Surprise First, Then Fight the Interest
_note: TEST FIXTURE B: invented example numbers (hypothetical), synthetic word timing generated from word length. Not research, not real voice.

scenes.narration: Your car breaks down on a Tuesday, and the repair is a surprise nobody planned for. Say it costs nine hundred dollars, and the only money you have is a credit card. That card charges twenty four percent interest a year. With no savings, the repair goes on the card, the interest piles up, and the debt keeps growing. Leave the balance alone for a year, and the interest alone is two hundred sixteen dollars. So the order you do things in matters more than the amount.

beats.narration: Your car breaks down on a Tuesday, and the repair is a surprise nobody planned for.
Say it costs nine hundred dollars, and the only money you have is a credit card.
That card charges twenty four percent interest a year.
With no savings, the repair goes on the card, the interest piles up, and the debt keeps growing.
Leave the balance alone for a year, and the interest alone is two hundred sixteen dollars.
So the order you do things in matters more than the amount.

scenes.narration: Here is the order. First, save a small buffer. Second, pay off the highest rate debt. Third, invest what is left. Compare what a dollar does. A savings account might pay four percent. A stock fund might average seven percent. The card costs twenty four. Watch the balance. Paying one hundred fifty dollars a month clears the card in about seven months. This week, list every balance and its rate. Set up one automatic transfer. Then pick the highest rate to attack first. Watch for three risks. A buffer that is too thin, a rate that changes, and a payment you forget. Cover the surprise first, then fight the interest.
